marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q001.takeaway: The femoral nerve is a lumbar-plexus branch formed from posterior divisions of L2–L4 ventral rami.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q001.displayText:
The femoral nerve is a lumbar-plexus branch formed from posterior divisions of L2–L4 ventral rami.

The femoral nerve is a branch of the lumbar plexus and arises from the posterior (dorsal) divisions of the ventral rami of L2-L4.

The sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, and nerve to obturator internus are part of the sacral plexus.
emphasis: The femoral nerve is a lumbar-plexus branch formed from posterior divisions of L2–L4 ventral rami

rationales.a: The sciatic nerve arises from the sacral plexus, not the lumbar plexus.
rationales.c: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is a sacral-plexus branch to posterior thigh skin.
rationales.d: The nerve to obturator internus is a sacral-plexus branch, not lumbar.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q002.takeaway: Meralgia paresthetica affects the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3), causing sensory symptoms without motor weakness.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q002.displayText:
Meralgia paresthetica affects the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3), causing sensory symptoms without motor weakness.

The scenario is suggestive of meralgia paresthetica, in which the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh is affected. Its root value is L2 and L3.

It arises from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami of L2 and L3 and supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the thigh up to the knee.
emphasis: Meralgia paresthetica affects the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3), causing sensory symptoms without motor weakness

rationales.a: L1–L2 does not match the usual lateral femoral cutaneous roots, which are L2–L3.
rationales.c: L1–L2–L3 adds an unsupported root; the source gives L2 and L3.
rationales.d: L2–L4 is the femoral nerve root range, whereas the purely sensory lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is L2–L3.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q003.takeaway: The sciatic nerve is the largest branch of the sacral plexus and exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q003.displayText:
The sciatic nerve is the largest branch of the sacral plexus and exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis.

The sciatic nerve is a branch of the sacral plexus. It is the largest branch of the sacral plexus.
emphasis: The sciatic nerve is the largest branch of the sacral plexus and exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis

rationales.a: Iliohypogastric nerve arises from L1 and is a lumbar-plexus/ventral-ramus branch.
rationales.b: Ilioinguinal nerve arises from L1, not the sacral plexus.
rationales.c: The obturator nerve arises from L2–L4 lumbar plexus, not sacral plexus.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q004.takeaway: The lateral circumflex femoral artery passes between femoral-nerve divisions as the nerve enters the thigh.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q004.displayText:
The lateral circumflex femoral artery passes between femoral-nerve divisions as the nerve enters the thigh.

The femoral nerve is split into anterior and posterior divisions by the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

Course of femoral nerve: it arises from posterior divisions of ventral rami of L2-L4 on the posterior abdominal wall, enters the femoral triangle under the inguinal ligament, lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath, and divides into anterior and posterior branches around the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

Source note: the obturator nerve is divided into anterior and posterior divisions by obturator externus in the upper part and adductor brevis in the lower part.
emphasis: The lateral circumflex femoral artery passes between femoral-nerve divisions as the nerve enters the thigh

rationales.a: Profunda femoris is a major deep arterial branch but is not the named vessel separating femoral-nerve divisions.
rationales.b: Deep external pudendal artery is a superficial femoral branch to external genital/perineal tissues, not the nerve divider.
rationales.d: Medial circumflex femoral artery curves posteriorly around the femoral neck and does not pass between these nerve divisions.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q005.takeaway: The nerve to pectineus arises from the femoral nerve near the inguinal ligament and passes deep to it behind the femoral sheath.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q005.displayText:
The nerve to pectineus arises from the femoral nerve near the inguinal ligament and passes deep to it behind the femoral sheath.

The nerve to pectineus arises near and passes below the inguinal ligament and then runs behind the femoral sheath.

The femoral nerve gives off nerves to iliacus and pectineus before dividing into anterior and posterior divisions.
emphasis: The nerve to pectineus arises from the femoral nerve near the inguinal ligament and passes deep to it behind the femoral sheath

rationales.a: The nerve to sartorius arises from the anterior division in the thigh, rather than passing below the ligament as the source describes.
rationales.b: The nerve to iliacus branches on the posterior abdominal wall before the femoral nerve passes under the inguinal ligament.
rationales.d: The nerve to rectus femoris is a muscular branch to quadriceps after the femoral nerve enters the thigh.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q006.takeaway: Gracilis is supplied by the obturator nerve, so its function is spared by an isolated femoral-nerve injury.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q006.displayText:
Gracilis is supplied by the obturator nerve, so its function is spared by an isolated femoral-nerve injury.

Gracilis is supplied by the obturator nerve and not the femoral nerve, so its function is not affected by femoral nerve injury.

Before entering the thigh, the femoral nerve supplies iliacus and pectineus. Its anterior division supplies sartorius and cutaneous branches to the anteromedial thigh. Its posterior division supplies quadriceps femoris, the knee joint, and sensation to the medial leg through the saphenous nerve.
emphasis: Gracilis is supplied by the obturator nerve, so its function is spared by an isolated femoral-nerve injury

rationales.a: Pectineus commonly receives femoral-nerve supply, although it may also receive obturator/accessory obturator branches.
rationales.c: Sartorius is innervated by the femoral nerve and can be affected by its injury.
rationales.d: Quadriceps femoris is supplied by femoral-nerve branches and knee extension is impaired with femoral neuropathy.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q007.takeaway: Femoral-nerve injury weakens quadriceps knee extension and reduces sensation over the anterior thigh.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q007.displayText:
Femoral-nerve injury weakens quadriceps knee extension and reduces sensation over the anterior thigh.

Loss of knee extension with decreased sensation over the anterior thigh suggests femoral nerve damage.

The femoral nerve innervates quadriceps femoris, the main extensors of the knee, and supplies sensation to the anterior and medial thigh through its cutaneous branches.
emphasis: Femoral-nerve injury weakens quadriceps knee extension and reduces sensation over the anterior thigh

rationales.a: The obturator nerve supplies most medial-thigh adductors, not quadriceps knee extensors or anterior-thigh sensation.
rationales.b: The common peroneal nerve supplies leg compartments and dorsiflexion/eversion, not anterior thigh or knee extension.
rationales.c: The tibial nerve supplies posterior leg/foot and hamstrings distally, not the described anterior-thigh territory.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q008.takeaway: The saphenous nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve's posterior division and supplies medial leg skin.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q008.displayText:
The saphenous nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve's posterior division and supplies medial leg skin.

Loss of sensation over the medial side of the leg denotes injury to the saphenous nerve, a branch of the posterior division of the femoral nerve.

The saphenous nerve is the largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve. It enters the adductor canal, crosses anterior to the femoral artery to lie medially, leaves the canal by piercing fascia lata between gracilis and sartorius, and then descends along the medial tibial border with the long saphenous vein.

It supplies the skin on the medial side of the knee, leg and foot as far as the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
emphasis: The saphenous nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve's posterior division and supplies medial leg skin

rationales.a: The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh, not the saphenous cutaneous territory along the medial leg.
rationales.c: The sural nerve supplies the posterolateral leg/lateral foot, not the medial leg around the saphenous vein.
rationales.d: The femoral anterior division supplies sartorius and anterior-thigh cutaneous branches; saphenous arises from the posterior division.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q009.takeaway: Adductor magnus is supplied by the posterior obturator division (and its hamstring part by tibial sciatic fibers), not the anterior division.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q009.displayText:
Adductor magnus is supplied by the posterior obturator division (and its hamstring part by tibial sciatic fibers), not the anterior division.

The anterior division of the obturator nerve does not innervate adductor magnus; adductor magnus is supplied by the posterior division.

The obturator nerve arises from anterior divisions of ventral rami L2-L4 and divides into anterior and posterior branches near the obturator foramen.

Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis and gracilis. Posterior division supplies adductor magnus and obturator externus, and may also supply adductor brevis.
emphasis: Adductor magnus is supplied by the posterior obturator division (and its hamstring part by tibial sciatic fibers), not the anterior division

rationales.a: Gracilis is supplied by the anterior division of the obturator nerve.
rationales.b: Adductor longus receives the anterior obturator division.
rationales.c: Adductor brevis is usually supplied by the anterior division, with posterior-division contribution possible.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q010.takeaway: The sciatic nerve supplies posterior-thigh muscles but does not innervate the gluteal muscles, which receive named gluteal or short-rotator nerves.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q010.displayText:
The sciatic nerve supplies posterior-thigh muscles but does not innervate the gluteal muscles, which receive named gluteal or short-rotator nerves.

The sciatic nerve does not innervate muscles of the gluteal region.

It is formed by L4-S3 components of the sacral plexus, exits through the greater sciatic foramen inferior to piriformis, descends in the posterior thigh and divides into tibial and common peroneal nerves proximal to the knee.

The tibial component supplies semimembranosus, semitendinosus, the ischial part of adductor magnus and long head of biceps femoris. The common fibular component supplies the short head of biceps femoris.
emphasis: The sciatic nerve supplies posterior-thigh muscles but does not innervate the gluteal muscles, which receive named gluteal or short-rotator nerves

rationales.a: The nerve to quadratus femoris supplies a deep gluteal-region external rotator.
rationales.b: The nerve to obturator internus supplies a deep external rotator in the gluteal region.
rationales.d: The nerve to piriformis directly supplies a deep gluteal muscle.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q011.takeaway: Left superior gluteal nerve injury weakens left gluteus medius/minimus, causing the contralateral pelvis to drop during right-leg lift.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q011.displayText:
Left superior gluteal nerve injury weakens left gluteus medius/minimus, causing the contralateral pelvis to drop during right-leg lift.

The gait shown is characteristic of a left superior gluteal nerve injury causing a positive Trendelenburg sign.

Gluteus medius and minimus are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. When the opposite leg is lifted, these abductors on the supported side raise the pelvis on the unsupported side and keep the trunk upright.

With paralysis, the pelvis sinks on the unsupported normal side when standing on the affected limb. In the figure, lifting the right leg causes the right side of the pelvis to tilt down, indicating a left-sided abductor mechanism lesion.

Inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus.
emphasis: Left superior gluteal nerve injury weakens left gluteus medius/minimus, causing the contralateral pelvis to drop during right-leg lift

rationales.a: Inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus; it does not produce the abductor weakness shown.
rationales.b: Right superior gluteal injury would cause pelvic instability on right stance, not the image's left-sided drop pattern.
rationales.c: Left inferior gluteal injury weakens gluteus maximus extension, not the hip abductors that maintain a level pelvis.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q012.takeaway: Common fibular (peroneal) neuropathy can paralyze anterior-compartment dorsiflexors and cause foot drop.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q012.displayText:
Common fibular (peroneal) neuropathy can paralyze anterior-compartment dorsiflexors and cause foot drop.

Foot drop is caused by damage to the common peroneal nerve.

The common peroneal nerve is a component of the sciatic nerve. It curves around the neck of the fibula deep to peroneus longus and divides into superficial and deep peroneal nerves.

The superficial peroneal nerve supplies peroneus longus and brevis and most of the dorsum of the foot. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the anterior compartment dorsiflexors, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei and the first web space.

Common peroneal injury causes weak dorsiflexion/foot drop, loss of eversion, loss of toe extension, and sensory loss over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot.
emphasis: Common fibular (peroneal) neuropathy can paralyze anterior-compartment dorsiflexors and cause foot drop

rationales.b: Femoral neuropathy affects knee extension and anterior thigh sensation rather than ankle dorsiflexion.
rationales.c: Tibial neuropathy weakens plantar flexors/intrinsic sole muscles; dorsiflexion is preserved.
rationales.d: Sciatic injury can cause foot drop if fibular fibers are involved, but the common fibular nerve is the direct lesion asked.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q013.takeaway: A common fibular nerve lesion at the fibular neck weakens dorsiflexion and eversion and can remove sensation over most of the dorsum of the foot.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q013.displayText:
A common fibular nerve lesion at the fibular neck weakens dorsiflexion and eversion and can remove sensation over most of the dorsum of the foot.

The affected nerve is the common fibular (common peroneal) nerve.

It is derived from L4, L5, S1 and S2 ventral rami through the sciatic nerve and runs along the lateral popliteal fossa to the fibular head, then winds around the fibular neck where it is commonly injured, including by a tight plaster cast.

It divides into superficial and deep fibular nerves. Injury produces foot drop, loss of eversion, loss of toe extension, and sensory loss over the anterolateral leg and dorsum of foot.

Source note: ankle reflex is preserved in common peroneal nerve palsy.
emphasis: A common fibular nerve lesion at the fibular neck weakens dorsiflexion and eversion and can remove sensation over most of the dorsum of the foot

rationales.a: Sural nerve injury affects the lateral foot and posterolateral calf, not the broad dorsal sensory and motor pattern described.
rationales.b: Superficial fibular injury causes eversion weakness and dorsal sensory loss but spares dorsiflexion by deep fibular branches.
rationales.c: Deep fibular injury weakens dorsiflexion but does not explain loss of sensation over the entire dorsum, including superficial-fibular territory.

marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q014.takeaway: Peroneus longus is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve; tibialis anterior, peroneus tertius and EDL receive deep fibular supply.
marrow__ANAT_CH57_Q014.displayText:
Peroneus longus is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve; tibialis anterior, peroneus tertius and EDL receive deep fibular supply.

Peroneus longus is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve; the other listed muscles are supplied by the deep peroneal nerve.

The anterior compartment of the leg is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve and includes tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and peroneus tertius.

The lateral compartment contains peroneus longus and brevis and is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. The posterior compartment is supplied by the tibial nerve.
emphasis: Peroneus longus is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve; tibialis anterior, peroneus tertius and EDL receive deep fibular supply

rationales.b: Peroneus tertius lies in the anterior compartment and is supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
rationales.c: Tibialis anterior is an anterior-compartment muscle supplied by deep fibular nerve.
rationales.d: Extensor digitorum longus is supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
